en: The sixth chapter: Death, like a conqueror seeking to gather his forces, repeatedly plucks from the earth those heroes who have been led away by secret emissaries dispatched by him.

The fault of treacherously slaying one who trusts him leads to the villain’s own destruction; it is like the sound of a young tree breaking, which steals away the sleep of an elephant and brings about the ruin of its heroism.

Then, when the twice-born man who had consumed the first funeral rice-ball (pretapiṇḍa) had eaten, when the distressing days of impurity (aśaucadivasa) had passed, and when the collection of royal requisites— such as beds, seats, chowries, sunshades, vessels, fans, and weapons— which caused a burning sensation to the eyes, was being bestowed upon the twice-born;

When the bones had been carried away along with the hearts of the people to sacred pilgrimage sites; when the funeral monument, a heap of white plaster serving as a memorial for the pyre, had become a thorn of grief;
and when the great war-elephant, Mahāvijitī, had been sent off to the forest;
And gradually, as the cries grew fainter, the lamentations became sparse, and the tears began to subside.
As the ears capable of hearing instruction grew slack, as the hearts worthy of attentive compliance became indifferent,
and as the royal virtues ceased to be counted;
The king had resorted to a state of existence limited to a mere region— confined to his grief, reduced to nothing but the lamentations of poets,
remaining only as a vision in dreams, surviving only in the heart, existing only as a figure in paintings, and persisting only as a name in poetry— when the lord of men passed away.

Once, King Harṣa, having suspended his affairs, saw himself unexpectedly surrounded by a multitude of his own kinsmen, led by a throng of elderly relatives who had gathered together, their faces bowed and silent.
Upon seeing this, he thought to himself, "What else can this mass of people, overwhelmed by grief, be signaling but that my noble brother has arrived?
With a trembling heart, he questioned a certain man of superior rank who was entering: "My friend, tell me!"
"Has the noble one arrived? he asked.

He replied softly, "My Lord, he is at the gate, as you commanded. Upon hearing this, his heart—though softened by the boundless grief born of fraternal affection—somehow did not abandon its life-force along with the surging flood of tears.

And immediately thereafter, [he was met] by a cry uttered by the attendants led by the gatekeeper who had entered first— like a wailing— and by a retinue whose numbers were diminished by their rapid journey from afar, with their umbrella-bearers scattered, their robe-carriers trailing, their water-pot holders fallen, their mouth-washing attendants dropped, their betel-bearers fainting, their sword-bearers limping, and consisting mostly of a few visible servants.
He was surrounded by an entourage whose bodies were darkened and emaciated from bathing, eating, and sleeping at intervals of many days;
his person was greyed by the incessant dust of the road, as if the earth itself had come to him for refuge, being left without a protector;

and his body was mottled with long, white bandages bound over wounds from arrow-gashes sustained in the battle to conquer the Hūṇas, appearing like the side-long glances of the approaching Goddess of Royal Fortune.

With limbs so emaciated as if they were pieces of flesh offered into the fire of grief for the sake of saving the life of the lord of the earth, he bore a burden of sorrow manifested by his wasted body;
on his head—bereft of its crest-jewel, with hair disheveled and soiled, and devoid of its floral ornament—he wore a crown of anguish that seemed to have taken physical form;
and he was marked by a broad forehead that, with streaks of sweat trickling from the heat, appeared to weep in longing to fall at the feet of his father.
He was incessantly drenching the earth—as if it were swooning from the death of her beloved husband—with a vast torrent of tears;
he bore cheeks that seemed hollowed out by the falling of an endless stream of tears, as if the two slopes of his face had been worn away by sorrow;
and he was distinguished by a lower lip whose betel-stain had melted away, as if dissolved by the exceedingly hot breath of his mouth.

He bore an ear-region that appeared darkened by the rays of sapphire, which were reduced to mere threads of sacred grass (*pavitrikā*), as if scorched by the great fire of grief born from the recent death of his father;

he was marked by a moon-like face whose features were indistinctly visible, yet which was encrusted with the garlands of rays from the blue pupils of his downcast, fixed eyes, appearing as if darkened by a beard grown thick with sorrow;
and he was like a lion overwhelmed by the fall of a great mountain, left without support.

It had become darkened, its splendor withered like the day when the sun has set; it was lusterless, like the Nandana grove when the celestial trees have been broken; it was empty, like a quarter of the sky when the elephants of the directions have departed.
Trembling like a mountain split by the fall of a heavy thunderbolt,
as if purchased by emaciation,
and as if enslaved by compassion.
As if enslaved by dejection,
as if made a pupil by grief,
as if blinded by mental anguish;
As if silenced by silence,
as if ground by pressure,
as if perspired by torment.
As if gathered up by anxiety,
as if dissolved by lamentation,
as if held fast by world-weariness;
As if rejected by analytical discernment,
as if despised by wisdom,
and as if cast far away by its invincibility.
Unattainable by those of aged intellect, incurable by those of well-spoken words, and inaccessible to the teachings of gurus.
It is impossible for the powers of the scriptures, an impassable path for the efforts of wisdom,
and beyond the range of the entreaties of friends.
He beheld his eldest brother swallowed by a grief that was out of place for the enjoyment of worldly objects and ungrounded for the accumulation of time’s passage;
and as if his entire body were being tossed up by a mass of surging waves of affection rising from agitation, he rose up, overcome by another's power.

Then, seeing him from afar, King Rājyavardhana, wishing to release the flood of tears accumulated over a long time, took him by his two long arms— stretched out so far as if encompassing all his sorrows— and, having clasped him to his neck, wept aloud again and again upon his emaciated chest where the silken garment had fallen away.
Placing his hands upon his throat, then upon his shoulders, and then within the hollows of his cheeks, he wept in such a manner that his hearts seemed to tear asunder from their bonds.
As if the veins of the streams of tears were released from his eyes, the world—having forgotten its king—along with the king’s favorites, wailed aloud as if in resonance.
After a long time, having somehow or other shed the water from his eyes, he himself grew calm, like a rain-cloud in autumn.

And having sat down, he washed his eyes— with some difficulty— using water brought by his attendants; the eyes, whose vision was stolen by their slow blinking as clusters of teardrops clung to the tips of his eyelashes, seemed to form streaks of foam upon a great flood of water due to the mass of rays from his fingernails, even though they were wiped again and again.
With a cloth provided by the betel-attendant, like a fragment of moonlight, he wiped his face which was scorched by the burning heat of his tears;
then, remaining silent for a long while, he rose and went to the bathing area.
Standing there, he carelessly wrung out his hair—disheveled and scattered—with his crest-ornament, while his lip quivered with the remnants of his grief.
As if wishing to live, and as if wishing to kiss with his lower lip even his own self made beautiful by the washing of the sea,

he performed the rite of worship to the deities of the quarters with the whiteness of his washed eyes— using, as it were, offerings of rows of petals from the clear beds of night-lotuses blooming at the rays of the autumnal moon—
and sat upon a couch placed on a four-pillared dais, provided with a single pillow resting against its headboard.
Having collapsed onto his couch, he remained silent;
King Harṣa likewise bathed and, with his body stretched out upon a rug laid upon the surface of the earth, stood nearby in silence.
As he gazed again and again at his father, whose entire being was consumed by anguish, it seemed as though his heart were bursting into a thousand pieces.
For the sight of the funeral pyre is the very youth of sorrow;
indeed, for the world, that day became even more dreadful than the day of the king's death.
Throughout the entire city, no one cooked, no one bathed, and no one ate.
Everywhere, everything wept;
by this process alone, the day passed away.

And the charioteer Aruṇa, crimson as madder, sank into the waters of the western ocean with a complexion reddened by the flow of thick blood and flesh from fresh wounds, like the body of Tvaṣṭṛ freshly hewn by the axe.
In the lotus lake, the swarm of bees hummed as they emerged from the buds of the closing lotuses;

and the circle of *cakravāka* birds, distressed by the pain of their imminent separation and tormented by longing, fixed tearful eyes upon the sun as it shone like a blossoming *bandhūka* flower, as if gazing at a kinsman.
As the goddess Śrī moved toward the bed of night-lotuses, which resounded with the humming of bees and was made beautiful by female swans, it tinkled like a network of ruby girdles and small bells.
The orb of the moon appeared in the sky, its dark spot clearly visible, resembling the hump of a bull belonging to Śaṅkara, mired in mud kicked up by its massive horns.
At that hour, being entreated by his chief vassals with words that could not be disregarded, he somehow or other took his meal.
When the night had turned to dawn and all the kings had entered, he spoke to Harṣadeva who was standing nearby: “Dear son,…”
"You are the ground for the execution of my father's commands. Even in your childhood, you grasped your father’s disposition like a banner of virtue;
therefore, my heart—driven by some cruel decree of fate—desires to speak this certain thing to you, who are so obedient."

Do not resort to this perverse obstinacy, which is easily found in the childish and is contrary to affection; do not, like a fool, create an obstacle to this desired goal. Listen, for you surely are not ignorant of the ways of the world.
When Māndhātṛ, the protector of the three worlds, had passed away, what was not accomplished by Purukutsa?
Or when Dilīpa, who ruled over the eighteen islands as directed by the creeper-like eyebrows [of his wife], had died, what was not achieved by Raghu?
And when Daśaratha, whose chariot was occupied by the gods in the midst of battle against the great asuras, had passed away, what was not performed by Rāma?
Has Dushyanta, by whom the four oceans were turned into mere cow-paddles, become a mere duṣyanta (a contemptible man) because of Bharata?

Let those matters rest for now; when our father—whose name was auspiciously invoked, whose age had been greyed by the spreading smoke of hundreds of sacrifices performed, and who was the very breath of Indra—passed away, why was the kingdom not taken by you?
Those learned in the scriptures say that he whom sorrow overcomes is a base man; for women are indeed the object of grief. Nevertheless, what can I do?
This is either a mark of cowardice or of femininity in one's own nature, that I have thus become the fuel for the fire of grief for my father.

For when my father had utterly collapsed, my tears flowed forth like mountain springs; when that great light had set, the ten directions became shrouded in darkness, the light of my wisdom was lost, and my heart burst into flames.
Discernment does not approach him even in his dreams, as if terrified of burning itself;
all his fortitude has melted away like lac under a powerful heat;
and his intellect falters at every step like a doe struck by a poisoned arrow.
Hope wanders from afar as if loathing a man, avoiding him; fortitude has gone away with her father, like a mother;
and [sorrows] increase day by day like the debts of a moneylender.
The body rains down a torrent of tears from its eyes, like a cloud produced from a mass of smoke from the fire of grief;
every person, having reached the state of the five elements, passes away.
"The world speaks falsely;
my father, though he has indeed attained the state of fire alone, does not burn me in this way.
Therefore, having seized my heart with this internal, as it were, concern for the hereafter, grief has arisen, difficult to restrain, like the submarine fire (*vāḍava*) upon the ocean."
Like a thunderbolt against a mountain, like a fire against the moon, and like Rāhu against the sun.
It burns me, tears me asunder, emaciates me, and devours me;
yet my heart is unable to pass the downfall of such a Great Being—who was like Mount Sumeru—by means of mere teardrops alone.
My eye has become averse to sovereignty, as if it were poison to a cakora bird.
My mind desires to abandon this ignoble fortune, which is like that of the Caṇḍālas—covered with many shrouds of the dead, stained with the colors of passion, and borne upon a bamboo pole;
I cannot endure to remain here for even a moment, like a bird in a burnt house.
Therefore, I wish to wash away this stain of affection, which clings to my heart like a garment, with the pure waters flowing from the mountain peaks and the clear streams at the hermitage.
Therefore, by the command of Puru, accept from me the burden of state affairs—just as one accepts old age, which, though undesirable, brings an end to the pleasures of youth;
let your chest be offered to Fortune like that of Hari when he abandoned all childhood play;
I have laid down my weapons."
Having spoken thus, he took his own sword from the hand of the sword-bearer and cast it upon the ground.

Then, hearing this, King Harṣa—struck as if by a sharp-pointed spear and with a heart rent asunder—reflected: "Could it be that the noble one has been provoked to anger by someone intolerant toward me, and has been made to believe some falsehood?"
"Is he desirous of testing me by this means?
Or is this a mental agitation in him born from grief for his father?
Or perhaps he is not even a noble person?"

What else was intended by the Noble One that I, with my faculty of hearing devoid of grief, have heard as something entirely different? Or rather, what else was the Noble One wishing to say that has emerged from his mouth as something quite contrary?
Or perhaps this is a device of Fate for the downfall of our entire lineage.
Is it the exhaustion of all my merit? Or is it the play of the entire circle of planets unfavorable to my actions?

Or perhaps it is the sport of the Kali age, which has become fearless regarding the destruction of my father, by which he treats me like some common person acting at random, as if I were not born of the lineage of Puṣyabhūti.
as if he were not his son,
as if he were not his younger brother,
as if he were not his devotee;
Though he was free from visible faults, he was like a Vedic scholar in the drinking of liquor,
like a good servant in betraying his master, like a virtuous man in associating with the base, and like a noble wife in her infidelity.
He has commanded me to perform an exceedingly difficult task.

Indeed, this is entirely appropriate: that when such a father—one who was like Mount Mandara for churning the ocean of the entire circle of vassal kings, intoxicated by the wine of the madness of valor—has died, one should either go to a forest of asceticism, take up bark garments, or practice austerities.
But that royal command directed toward me— though I am already consumed— is like a rain of embers upon a forest parched by drought;
it is unbecoming of my noble brother,
even though he is all-powerful and free from pride.
A twice-born man is one who is free from desire; a sage is one who is free from anger; a monkey is one who is not fickle.
A poet free from envy, a merchant who does not steal, a husband devoted to his wife and free from deceit,
and a virtuous man who is not poor.
A wealthy man who is not wicked,
a miser who does not come before one's eyes,
and a hunter who is non-violent.
A Brahmin born of Parāśara, a servant who is happy,
and a gambler who is grateful.
A wandering mendicant who does not seek enjoyment, a cruel man who speaks kindly,
and a minister who speaks the truth.
A prince who is not ill-behaved is rare indeed in this world;
nevertheless, my noble father alone is my teacher.

For when such a father—a scent-elephant of royalty—has fallen, who indeed would take up the burden of instruction while his own arms, once as sturdy as massive stone pillars, have been rendered fruitless?

When the elder brother, the lord of the earth, having renounced the kingdom in his youth, was departing for the forest of asceticism, even an outcaste would have desired that lump of clay called "the Earth"— which is impure from the falling tears of the eyes of all people— and that female slave named "Fortune" (Śrī), belonging to the household of the noble warriors, whose low conduct is proclaimed by the facial distortions of every villain reeling with the intoxication of wealth.
How could my noble brother have conceived such an utterly improper thought?
What impure mark has he perceived in me?
Or has Saumitri fallen from his mind, or have Vṛkodara and the others been forgotten?
Such sovereign power as this never belonged to our noble lord—he who was indifferent to his dependents and harsh in his sole devotion to accomplishing his own ends.
Moreover, once the noble one had departed for the forest of asceticism, who, desiring to live, would even in thought covet the earth?

[For it was] a face radiant with a mass of beautiful manes, sprinkled by the spray of rut from the finest elephants, which had been shattered by a volley of blows from claws as fierce as the tips of thunderbolts.

When the lion has gone out for a stroll in the forest, who remains behind to guard the mountain cave that is his dwelling? For those possessed of courage have valor as their only companion. And what is this misplaced concern of yours, O Noble One, toward the fickle Goddess of Royal Fortune, if she too—her breasts no longer veiled by her garment—is carrying a bundle of kusha grass, flowers, sacrificial fuel, and palāśa leaves right there in that penance grove like a wild doe?
"Old age, like a net, is leading her away.
What is the use of my fruitless and manifold deliberations? I shall simply follow the Noble One in silence.
Furthermore, this transgression committed by disobeying the words of my elder will surely be expiated by asceticism in the forest of penance."
Having thus resolved in his mind, he went first to the penance grove and stood there silently with his head bowed down.
In the meantime, when the bark garments had been presented by the weaver who was weeping as previously instructed,
his heart departed somewhere, as if out of fear of being struck mercilessly by the palm of his hand.
The king’s women shrieked;
the Brahmins raised their arms and cried out with loud cries of "Un-Brahmanly!";
and the crowd of citizens, intent on prostrating at his feet, groaned aloud.
When the long-standing attendants had fled with their hearts in a panic,
and the eldest kinsman had departed supported by his followers,
his body trembling;
With her garments in disarray,
her speech faltering with grief, and tears streaming from her eyes,
While the circle of kinsmen was intent on dissuading him,
and while the vassal lords— despairing and with faces cast downward— were sighing upon the jeweled floors scratched by their fingernails;

When all the subjects, including the young and the old, had set out for the penance grove, the most famous attendant of the royal fortune named Saṃvādaka suddenly entered, overwhelmed with grief, his eyes streaming with tears; having ceased his wailing, he threw himself down before the assembly.
Then the Lord Rājyavardhana himself, greatly agitated, questioned him along with his brother: “Good man!
Speak, speak! Why are you so intent on increasing our misfortune and resolve? Why do you rejoice at the death of the king?”
"Fate brings about another even greater lack of fortitude, leading to an exceeding intensity of suffering.
He said with great difficulty,
"Your Majesty, the conduct of those with base souls, like that of Piśācas, generally consists of striking at one's vulnerabilities."

On the very day the report spread that the lord of the earth had passed away, the noble Grahaveṛma was made by the evil-minded King of Mālava to depart from the world of the living along with his own merit.

And the princess Rājyaśrī, her feet kissed by a pair of fetters of black iron, was cast into prison at Kānyakubja like a female thief. Furthermore, there is a rumor that the wicked-minded one, perceiving the army to be without a leader, desires to seize it and intends to invade this land as well.
When this had been thus reported, [the king thought], "The lord has power.

And so, having heard of such an unexpected, improbable, and sudden calamity above, because it was something never before heard of and because of his own nature's intolerance for the humiliation of others, [he was moved].
Due to the abundance of pride characteristic of fresh youth, his birth from a lineage of heroes,
and out of affection for his sister who was an object of compassion, that surge of grief— though so firmly rooted and exceedingly heavy— vanished for him in an instant.
And suddenly, a terrifying surge of anger entered his deep heart like a lion entering the dwelling of a mountain cave.

Upon the broad surface of his forehead, a formidable frown emerged, darkening as if it were the sister of Yama; it was wavy with the knitting of brows that were as crooked as Kāliya’s when he was agitated by the fear of the slayer of Keśin.

As he stroked [his arm] out of pride, his left hand—resembling the frontal globes of a world-elephant—performed, as it were, an inauguration for the burden of battle with the waterfalls of light from his fingernails.

His belly filled with trickling sweat, trembling as if his hair had been seized root and all for the uprooting of Mālava, or out of a longing to grasp the locks of Durmada’s Fortune, his other hand again brandished its terrifying sword. A tawny flush of rage appeared upon his cheeks, like the vermilion dust shaken from the brow by the Goddess of Royal Fortune as she rose to seize his weapon— a sign of her good fortune.
As if conceiving pride from the act of treading upon the circle of crest-jewels of all the neighboring kings, he raised his right foot, with its sole turned upward, onto the left thigh.
With his other lotus-foot, from which lines of smoke were blown out by the friction of his hard big toe, he scratched the jeweled floor as if releasing a flame to strip the earth of its heroes.

As if awakening his younger brother Parākrama—who was slumbering in the poison of grief—with sprinklings of blood spurting from fresh wounds burst open by his own arrogance, he said: “Long-lived one!...”
This is the royal palace;
these are my kinsmen;
this is my retinue.
"This is the land, and these are the subjects protected by the arm-staffs of the king;
I myself am departing this very day for the destruction of the royal house of Mālava."
This very act of donning bark garments is indeed penance, and this alone is the means for dispelling grief: the suppression of utterly undisciplined enemies.
Yet this is like seizing a lion by the mane with fawns, or striking a black cobra with frogs.
The capture of a tiger by calves,
the throttling of a Garuḍa by water-snakes,
and the ordering of a fire to burn with pieces of wood— these are [impossible].
Just as the sun is obscured by cataracts,
so too has the humiliation of the Puṣyabhūti dynasty by the Mālavas been eclipsed by my own great indignation.
"Let all the kings and elephants remain with you alone;
let this Bhaṇḍi follow me with a mere ten thousand horses.
Having spoken thus, he immediately ordered the drum of march to be beaten.

Hearing him thus instructing [him], King Harṣa, his mind tormented by the indignation arising from the knowledge of the conduct of his sister and brother-in-law, spoke as if pained by the deep-rooted affection he felt at the command for her return: "What fault indeed does my noble brother see in my following him?"
If I am indeed a child, then I must certainly not be abandoned;
if I am one who requires protection, then the cage of your arms is my place of refuge; and as for being called "incapable," by whom have I been so examined?
Thinking "he must be nurtured," separation makes him thin; thinking "he cannot endure hardship," I have been entrusted to the care of women;
thinking "let him experience happiness," that very happiness departs along with you.
The hardship of the long journey is more unbearable than the fire of separation; "protect your wife"—thus Fortune dwells upon your sword;
"it is empty behind"—thus your majesty remains indeed [unassailable].
"Since it is not presided over by the King, it is well-bound by the virtues of the noble;
since there is no external companion for one of great stature, he counts me as something separate;
and as I depart with but a very light retinue, what excessive burden could there be in the dust of my feet?"
"It is improper for the two of us to go; favor me, therefore, with permission to depart.
To think that affection for a brother is cowardice is a fault consistent with your character.
And what is this self-centeredness of yours, O arm, that you alone thirst for fame as white as the mass of foam from the milk-ocean, as if it were nectar?"
"I have never before been deceived in matters of grace;
therefore, may your honor be gracious and lead me as well.
Having spoken thus, he cast his head upon the surface of the earth and fell at [his] feet.
Having raised him up, the elder spoke again:
"Father, why is such great weight imposed by force upon this most insignificant and harmful undertaking through the assumption of such a massive enterprise?
This accumulation of resources for a lion, undertaken for the sake of a deer, is utterly shameful."
How many fires can quickly consume mere blades of grass?
Moreover, the entire earth, garlanded with the eight auspicious islands, is indeed within the scope of your valor;
for winds capable of sweeping away the mass of great mountains do not exert their force against a most fragile heap of cotton.
Neither do celestial elephants, arrogant in their intimacy with Mount Sumeru, submit to a tiny anthill;

nor will you seize, for the conquest of the quarters, my bow—which bears ornaments of beautiful golden lotus-petal vines and is like a great comet portending the dissolution of all earthly lords—just as Māndhātṛ did.
But while this hunger of mine to destroy the enemy is uncontrollable and agitated, let this one mouthful of wrath from me, who am alone, be forgiven.
"May you remain," he said, and on that very day he departed for the enemy's territory. Now, when his brother had thus gone,
When his father had passed away, when his son-in-law’s life was spent abroad, and when his mother had died,

And while his sister was thus restrained, King Harṣa, like a wild elephant strayed from his herd, passed that time somehow or other all alone. When many days had elapsed, once during the final watch of the night—while he remained awake due to the sorrow of his brother’s departure—he heard this Āryā verse being recited by a sentry: “Even the moon, though it possesses a cool nature, becomes hot to the eyes of one who has been separated from his beloved; how much more so, then, the fire of separation?”* *Note: The original Sanskrit verse is: *api candanaviṭapī jvalati hutavahastuhinadīdhitirapi ca tāpayati gātram | api nalinamapi śiśirakiraṇasya raśmirvirahī kimiva na viṣaheta viṣahīnam ||* (Even the sandalwood tree burns with fire, and even the moon of cool rays causes the body to suffer heat; even the lotus is scorched by the ray of the moon—what indeed cannot a man separated from his beloved endure when deprived of her?)* Upon hearing this, the king, whose heart was already tormented by the fire of grief for his brother, felt as if he were being struck by a thunderbolt. He thought to himself: "Alas! Even the moon, which is the very essence of coldness, brings heat to the eyes of one separated from his beloved; how much more so, then, the fire of separation! Having reflected thus, and having resolved to depart for the city of Kanyakubja, he immediately summoned his minister named Śukanāsa. Once the minister had arrived, the king spoke to him: "O Śukanāsa, you know the entire course of my life from its very beginning. Since my birth, I have never experienced even a moment's separation from my kinsmen. Now, however, I am separated from both my father and my sister. Therefore, I wish to go to the city of Kanyakubja to see my elder brother, the illustrious Rājyavardhana. Hearing this, the minister replied: "Your Majesty, this is not the time for such a journey. For the present, the army is stationed on the banks of the Gaṅgā, having set out from the city of Thanesar. Furthermore, the illustrious Rājyavardhana has recently returned from the land of the Turks and is currently staying in the city of Sthāneśvara. It is said that he intends to march against the king of Gauda, who has rebelled against him. Therefore, let Your Majesty first proceed to the city of Sthāneśvara and remain there until the return of the victorious prince. Then, after seeing the elder brother, you may set out for Kanyakubja at your leisure. The king, however, did not accept these words. Instead, he dismissed the minister and, accompanied only by a few horsemen, set out toward the city of Sthāneśvara. As he traveled, he reached a certain forest on the way. There, he beheld a woman of celestial beauty sitting beneath a tree, weeping bitterly. She was adorned with ornaments of pearls and gems, wearing a single braid of hair, and clad in garments of white silk. Seeing her, the king, overcome with compassion, approached her and asked: "Who are you, O lady? Why do you weep so? She, for her part, wiped away her tears and, bowing low, replied: "O noble sir, I am the daughter of King Tārāpīḍa of Kāmarūpa, named Malayavatī. My father, having been defeated in battle by the illustrious Rājyavardhana, has gone to the city of Sthāneśvara to seek refuge with him. I, however, being unable to bear the sight of my father's distress, have come here to this forest to end my life. But alas! Fate is cruel, and my desire is frustrated. Hearing this, the king said: "O lady, do not act rashly. I myself shall go to the city of Sthāneśvara and bring about your reunion with your father. With these words, he consoled her and departed. Reaching the city of Sthāneśvara, he saw the illustrious Rājyavardhana seated upon a jeweled throne, surrounded by his ministers. Approaching him, the king prostrated himself at his feet and announced his arrival. The prince, seeing him, rose up with great affection and embraced him. Having offered him a seat and water for his feet, he asked: "O brother, why have
Fate suddenly casts down a man, just as the wind strikes a ship— even one whose virtues are celebrated by the islands and which carries the essence of a hoarded heap of jewels.
Having heard that, his heart was further tormented by the contemplation of impermanence; when most of the night had passed, he obtained sleep for but a moment.
And in a dream, he saw a pillar of iron reaching to the clouds being shattered;
with a trembling heart, he woke up once more.
And he thought:
"Why indeed do these evil dreams constantly pursue me? And my left eye throbs day and night, foreboding ill fortune."
Most terrible and no longer minor, these portents do not subside for even a moment, foretelling the destruction of the king’s faction.
Every day, Rāhu is observed seizing the solar disc as if with his full body intact, while it remains headless.
The Seven Sages vomit forth columns of smoke, as if their very ascetic power had been swallowed by Time, turning all the planets a sooty grey.
Day after day, terrible conflagrations of the quarters are seen;
the host of stars falls from the vault of heaven like a shower of sparks from the ashes of a burning direction.
As if in grief over the falling of the stars, the moon has lost its luster.
Night after night, the quarters of the sky, with their flickering stars, seem to behold a fierce battle of planets in the firmament by means of meteors blazing here and there.

A wind, carrying a mass of thick dust and making a whistling sound as it tosses fragments of gravel, seems to traverse the earth like an omen portending a transfer of sovereignty. I do not perceive any auspiciousness in this conjunction.
"Who could be an adversary to Death, who—like an elephant toward a *karīra* sapling—regards even the tenderest thing in this lineage of ours as fragile?
In every way, may it be well with my noble brother.

Having thought this, and having with great difficulty steadied his heart—which was inwardly shattered by the pangs of brotherly affection and seemed to melt away—he rose and performed the customary round of duties as they were prescribed.
And having reached the assembly hall, he suddenly saw him entering,
followed by a dejected-looking crowd who were following behind him;
his body was shrouded in a soiled garment that appeared as if its red threads were smoke from unbearable, hot sighs of grief.
With his face bowed down as if out of shame for continuing to live,

his gaze fixed on the tip of the bridge of his nose, Kuntala— a high-ranking horse-attendant— was making his master’s misfortune known through a silent face whose hair had grown long from grief, by means of incessant teardrops.
He beheld the most familiar site of Rājyavardhana’s favor;
and upon seeing it, apprehension arose within him, manifesting as moisture in his eyes and sighs from his moon-like face.

At that moment of hearing the dreadful and unpleasant news, he was seized simultaneously by the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in his heart by Fire, and in his lap by Earth; all his limbs were gripped at once.

Furthermore, he heard that his brother—though he had effortlessly defeated the Mālava army—had been treacherously murdered in his own palace by the Lord of Gauḍa, who, having fostered confidence through false pretenses, killed him while he was alone, unarmed, and trusting.
Upon hearing this, the one of great majesty suddenly blazed up, his surge of grief being fanned by the spreading fire of his fierce anger.

Then, as if his body were marked by fragments of crest-jewels shattered from his head shaking in indignation, he vomited forth the fire of his wrath; with his eyes reddening and rolling in rage, he seemed to drink up the lifespans of all the powerful through their incessant throbbing, while the flickering glances of his bloodshot eyes displayed, as it were, conflagrations across the quarters of the sky.
A foul day was created by the showers of sweat-droplets spreading forth as if scorched by the unbearable heat of his innate heroism burning with the fire of wrath;
he was accompanied by his own limbs, which were trembling as if terrified by an anger never seen before,
and he assumed a terrifying form like Hara himself.
Like Hari manifesting the form of Narasimha,
like a sun-stone mountain ignited by the sight of the spreading radiance of another fire,
and like the day of universal destruction when one's form becomes difficult to behold due to the rising of twelve suns;
Like a great cataclysmic wind causing the trembling of all mountains,
like the Vindhya range whose physical height increases ever more,
and like a great venomous serpent provoked by the oppression of a wicked king;
Like Parīkṣit, he was intent on consuming all serpents; like Vṛkodara, he was thirsting for the blood of his enemies;
like the celestial elephant, he rushed toward the opposing tuskers; and like the primordial source of manly valor.
Like madness of intoxication, like agitation of pride,
like the descent of youth upon splendor.
Like a total exertion of pride,
like the arrival of a new age for the heat of youth,
like the consecration of a kingdom for the passion for battle.
On that day, which was like a day of lustration for intolerance, it reached the height of terror.

And he said: "O base lord of Gauḍa, who but you would abandon such a great man at that very moment—him who had instantly conquered the entire circle of kings with his sincere strength of arm—and thus cause this noble one, who has laid down his weapons like Agastya, to be extinguished by such a death as this, which crushes all the world of heroes?"

And who, having abandoned that ignoble man, would not feel partiality in their hearts— white as the mass of foam on the Bhāgīrathī— for those who proclaim the heroism of the noble one, acting like royal swans in lakes at the mere memory of Paraśurāma’s prowess? How is it that his hands, so exceedingly fierce in taking the life of the noble one, have been extended without regard for affection, like the rays of the summer sun in drying up the waters of a lotus pond?
To what destiny will he go, or into what womb will he enter, or in which hell will he fall?
"Who but a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*) would do such a thing?

Even as I utter the name of this evildoer, my tongue seems as if stained by the impurity of his sin. Having undertaken what task did that noble one allow himself to be entered by that vile, pitiless wretch, who has brought him—who was like a pillar of sandalwood, expert at delighting the entire world—to destruction, just as a wood-boring insect (*ghuṇa*) destroys its host?"
"Surely this fool, greedy for the taste of sweetness and drawing in the honey of noble life as if it were mere liquor, did not foresee the calamity of the swarm of arrows that would fall upon him.

This lowest of the Gauḍas, acting as a lamp on the path to his own house’s ruin, has accumulated nothing but an exceedingly dark infamy, like soot. Even though the sun—the crest-jewel of the three worlds—had already set, the Creator ordained the moon, the sole lord of the deer roaming the forest of the planets, to suppress the darkness that is the enemy of the path of truth."
Śaśī said:

"O establisher of discipline, even when the goad is broken, there still exists for the purpose of subduing a wild elephant the exceedingly cruel claw of a lion, which can split the firm frontal globes of all rutting elephants; who would not put to death such wicked lapidaries who destroy precious gems?"
"Where now will this wretch go?

Even as his father was speaking thus, the general— who was a friend of his father, the foremost in all military engagements, whose body was as bright as a mountain of yellow orpiment, who possessed the appearance of a mature and straight trunk of a *sāla* tree,
and who had reached the fullness of maturity through the very heat of his exceeding valor— was present, existing at an advanced age.
Though he had just risen from his bed of many arrows, he seemed to be smiling at the extreme longevity of Śāntanu;
for even old age, as if terrified by his invincible body, touched him with manifest trembling, while he—

with some effort— transferred into his strong hair a lion-like state, white as a mass of moonbeams and thick with straight locks, composed of the essence of guileless valor, as if it were a second birth while still alive.
His vision was obscured by a pair of eyebrows that were curled and covered with loose, hanging skin, as if wishing to avoid the great sin of looking upon the face of another’s master;

with his formidable face—its cheeks brightened by being veiled in white, thick tufts of hair—he seemed to be vomiting forth, even out of season, the onset of autumn, pure as a blossoming grove of *kāśa* grass during the time of his own prowess;
and he possessed a long, hanging mass of beard that fanned his deceased lord, as it were, with a white chowrie held close to his heart.
Even in his later years, his broad chest was made uneven by large, gaping wounds that seemed like mouths opened wide in thirst to drink the water from the edge of a whetted sword-blade;

and because of the dense rows of thick scars on his many arms, carved by the tips of sharp weapons and chisels, he appeared like a walking eastern mountain counting the successive victories of all his battles,
as if he were making even the *Mahābhārata* seem insignificant with the charm of his various heroic exploits.
As if instructing even Paraśurāma through his persistent application in destroying the adversaries;
as if making even Mount Mandara sluggish with the grace of his effortless drawing away of the Goddess of Fortune;
and as if surpassing even the ocean by following the discipline of the leaders of armies.

As if putting even the mountains to shame by the heights of his steady sun-like majesty; as if treating even the sun as a mere blade of grass through the flashing radiance of his innate and fierce brilliance;
and as if laughing at even the bull of Śiva because his back was so accustomed to bearing the weight of the Lord.
The firestick for the fire of indignation,
sovereignty for valor,
and the spreading of a rash for pride.
The heart of *haṭha* (forceful effort),
the life-breath of the desire to conquer, and the very respiration of enthusiasm.
He is a goad for the intoxicated, a subduer of serpents for wicked beings,
and the cessation of the state of being a superior man.
He was the family preceptor of the assemblies of heroes, the scale for those possessed of valor,
and the one who had seen the very limits of the entire arsenal of weapons.
He was the fulfiller of bold declarations,
the restorer of those who had been broken,
and one who reached the further shore of his promises.

An expert in the vital points of great battles, a drum for the proclamation of those seeking war, Siṃhanāda sat right there nearby; with a voice as deep as the sound of a kettledrum, he announced to the brave warriors, rousing their passion for combat: [The rest of the text follows...]
“Your Majesty, just as crows, like base men, do not realize they are being deceived by a soiled cuckoo that has taken up residence with them and become even more filthy,
for the defects of fortune— blindness and other such disorders— are indeed like jaundice.
Those of dull intellect, their own splendor shielded by the shadow of the royal parasol, forget any other person of brilliance.”

What indeed can that wretch do, he who, out of extreme cowardice, is perpetually turned away from battle? For he has never seen the faces of enraged, spirited men—faces whose fire of wrath blossoms with the bristling of hair on tawny cheeks, swollen by a surfeit of valor that surpasses all others. That poor fellow does not know that high-minded men, when provoked, bring about the immediate destruction of an entire lineage, just like malevolent spells.
Even in water, those who possess inner fire blaze when struck;
such an act—skilled at hurling one into the bottomless depths of hell—is truly worthy only of him who is excluded from the assembly of all heroes.

For when the bow, the preeminent wealth of the spirited, is being wielded, and the sword, which is a pleasure-grove of blue lotuses for the swan-like Lakṣmī, is present, then methods such as churning the ocean are but the stratagems of the wretched.
How much less so for those such as these?

For how could those possessed of mighty arms— who, though the Creator himself was unable to protect the earth, were appointed by him as its guardians, and who even cause mountains to vomit forth iron for the sake of striking with their club-like, lineage-hardened arms— ever contemplate an unworthy deed even in their minds, they who are the kinsmen of stainless fame?
Indeed, before the rays from the hands of great warriors, which are radiant in their conquest of all planetary influences, the rays of the sun are but cripples in grasping the quarters of the sky.

The southern direction, whose interior is terrifying with the jagged breaking of waves from the horns of great buffaloes, is merely a matter of popular convention; in ultimate reality, it is the abode of Yama, the frown upon the brow of a warrior.
And it is a marvel that when heroes let out lion-roars in battles, their manes do not fly out along with the mass of bristling hair caused by the sudden thrill of reckless impetuosity.

Only two things are capable of containing the mass of prosperity gathered from the four oceans: either the terrible submarine fire that consumes its opposite, or the heart of a Great Man. For how could there be any cessation of the heat belonging to a radiant being, which is born together with the ocean? The Lord of Serpents, who bears a vast burden of expanded hoods in vain, carries in his coils nothing but a mere lump of clay.
However, only the arms of heroes—whose forearms shine with the weight of the world’s elephants—know the flavor of the pleasure derived from enjoying the conquest of unimpeded commands.
Like the sun, whose foot-stalks are grasped by the beds of upturned lotuses, the hero passes his days in ease with undiminished splendor.
But for the coward, whose heart is like the deer-marked moon and whose back is pale, fortune remains motionless for not even two nights.
The heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) expands, raining down a multitude of immeasurable glories;
the paths of manly prowess are cleared by his advancing majesty;
and the gates of pride become open, as enemies are driven away by his roar.
The empty quarters of the sky are illuminated by the light of his weapons;
the earth, as it were, is colored with the spray of his enemies' blood, and so too is his royal fortune.
By being ground upon the whetstone edges of the crest-jewels of many kings, his row of toenails, as it were, makes even his silver radiance blaze forth.
Through the constant practice of weapons, even the faces of enemies turn dark as if they were the palms of one's own hands;

and by the hundreds of bandages bound over various wounds, one’s fame becomes white as if it were one’s own body. As arrows are cast down upon the chest-panels of armored enemies, [they become fixed there].
Cruel sword-strokes vomit forth glory like the crest of a flame;
yet the high-minded man whose own kin have been slain by the enemy expresses his heart’s sorrow by striking the breasts of his foes’ wives.
He sighs with the wind from the fall of harsh sword-blades and weeps with the eyes of the women of the opposing side at the onset of the breathless torrent of falling enemies.
He who gives water is superior, not the other;
for the awakened do not bind their sense of kinship to momentary bodies as if they were things lost upon waking from a dream.
To the brave, the notion of a body is fixed upon it as if it were enduring fame.

And just as soot and grime do not touch a jewel-lamp whose very nature is radiant with a continuous spreading of blazing splendor, so too does grief not touch one who is exceedingly resplendent. You are the foremost among the courageous, the leader of the wise, the first among the capable, the chief of the noble-born, and the head of the indomitable. Furthermore, these [arms] of yours are ever at your command—lands cooled by the dwelling of fortitude, sheltered by the forest-shade of your formidable arms, satisfied by the water of the edge of the sword that is easily grasped, and wherein the fire of anger smokes only when constantly provoked.
"What is the use of this lowest of Gauda lords?
Act in such a way that no one else ever behaves like this again.
Let the fly-whisks of all those who desire the faith of the entire earth—those false seekers of victory—be waved by the sighs of the women of the inner apartments."
Cut away the calamities of the royal parasol’s shade with the veiling of circles of vultures blinded by the scent of blood;
dispel the feverish passion of the eyes of the unfaithful Fortune of the lineage with the baths of lukewarm water of gore;
and allay the swellings of the rash of reckless valor with the piercing wounds of sharp arrow-heads.

Uproot the painful affliction of iron shackles with the great medicinal herbs that are [the sight of] your stainless feet; dispel the numbness of those feet, which have become calloused from the longing for footstools;
soothe the itching in the ears caused by hearing the word "victory" with the application of the caustic salt of harsh commands;
and remove the deformities of the stiff, unbending necks by smearing the foreheads with the sandalwood paste of the radiance of your toenails.
Extract the thorns of the playful conduct of the wicked, which are smoldering with the heat of pride in wealth, using the pincers of commands for the collection of taxes;
shatter the darkness of the frowning brows of arrogant, veteran warriors with the brilliant lamps of the radiance from your jeweled footstool;
and conquer the great calamities of false pride by means of the fierce gravity of those whose head-pomp has fallen away through the agility of your treading upon their heads.
Tenderize those calluses of hardness formed by the scars of the bowstring, which were heated by the palms of your hands joined in constant service like cupped lotus buds;
do not abandon that very path desired by the three worlds, along which your father, grandfather, and great-grandfather have gone.
Casting off this grief befitting a base man, take up the royal fortune inherited through your lineage, like a lion seizing a doe.

"O Lord, now that the King has passed into the state of divinity, and since Rājyavardhana’s life has been consumed by the wicked serpent of Gauḍa, this great dissolution having occurred, you alone remain as the Śeṣa to uphold the earth.
Console the subjects who are without refuge;
set your foot upon the heads of kings like the autumn sun scorching their foreheads."

Attain the state of Kalmāṣapāda by means of the circles of smoke from your sighs—scorched by the pain of initiation into the service of those who are harmful—and by the rising rays of the crest-jewels of your enemies, which burn like fire.
Furthermore, while your father was slain, you were a solitary ascetic, reared among deer, with a mind naturally soft and delicate due to your Brahmin birth;

yet now, you have resolved to make the elephants of the quarters lose their pride with the roar of the twanging of your fierce bow, and to bring fever to the world with the humming of your drawn bowstring.

Paraśurāma uprooted the entire Kṣatriya host twenty-one times when they rose up together; how much more so, then, can Your Majesty, the crest-jewel of the proud, whose mind is like a thunderbolt due to its natural physical hardness?

Therefore, having made your vow this very day, take up your bow—the banner of a sudden expedition marked by the signs of compassion for the wretched Kāla, who is agitated by the collection of the life-force of the base lord of Gauḍa, in order to destroy his life.

Indeed, this most terrible fever of the burning pain of grief does not subside for Your Majesty—whose body is being scorched by the fire of humiliation—without the cooling treatment of being anointed with red sandalwood paste from the enemy’s blood.

For when all means to pacify the torment of insult had been exhausted, the Son of the Wind (Bhīma) drank the nectar of the enemy’s blood as if it were the taste of Hiḍimbā’s kisses, employing no method other than that; and the son of Jamadagni (Paraśurāma), finding the touch of the lakes formed from the blood of Kṣatriyas cool and pleasant to the feverish flames of his quenching wrath, bathed therein.
Having said this, he ceased speaking.
But the god Harṣa replied to him:
"What has been stated by your honor is indeed something that must be done."

Otherwise, even while the Lord of Serpents occupies the ground seized by me, the creeper-like brow of my envious arm moves upward, as if casting a glance at an heir; and even toward the host of planets passing overhead, the creeper-like brow of my envious arm moves upward, desiring to strike them down as if they were rival claimants.
His hand desires to seize by the hair even those mountains that refuse to bow;
his heart longs to make even the sun’s rays—arrogant with their brilliance—into whisks;
and his foot seeks to make even the heads of the lions who bear the title of "King" into footstools.

My lower lip quivers even to issue a command or a decree to the world-protectors, who are subject to their own whims; how much more so now that such a wretch has been born, and when my mind is overflowing with indignation? Indeed, there is no room at all for the performance of funeral rites. Moreover, while this vile, wretched, and world-despised Caṇḍāla, the lord of Gauḍa—a scoundrel who is a sharp thorn in my heart and deserves to be crushed by a mace—is still alive, I am ashamed to even hiss in grief like a snake, my lips parched and devoid of any means of retaliation.
For me, who have not yet brought down a rain of tears from the tremulous eyes of the wives of my enemies' forces, how can there be the offering of water from my two hands?
And for my eyes, which have not yet beheld the circles of smoke from the funeral pyres of that lowest of the Gauḍas, how can there be even a drop of tear-water?
Hear my vow:
"I swear by the touch of the dust from the noble one's very feet:

if within a counted number of days I do not rid the earth of the Gauḍas— making the feet of all kings, who are arrogant with the fickleness of their bows, jingle with fetters— then, like a moth in clarified butter, may I, a sinner, cast myself into the fire."
Having said this, he commanded Avantika, the chief minister of peace and war who was standing nearby:
"Let it be written:
from the Eastern Mountain, whose peaks are abandoned by pairs of *cāraṇa* sages startled by the creaking of the wheels of the sun’s chariot..."
From Suvela, where the events of the plundering of Laṅkā by the descendant of Kakutstha are inscribed upon the peaks, ridges, and slopes of its three summits;
from the western mountain [Astagiri], whose cavernous belly resounds with the tinkling of the anklets of Varuṇa’s excellent wives stumbling under the influence of wine;

and from Gandhamādana, whose cave-dwellings are scented by fragrant aromatic stones perfumed by the scent of the wives of the Guhyakas—let the hands of all kings be prepared for the payment of tribute and for the grasping of weapons.
Let the quarters of the sky take up fly-whisks, let heads bow or bows bend,
and let commands be made into ear-ornaments or bowstrings.
Let the dust of his feet become crest-jewels or helmets;
let the joining of palms be formed like the trappings of a herd of elephants; let the earth be released or arrows be discharged.
Let cane-sticks or spear-staffs be grasped;
let yourselves be well observed either in my toenails or in the mirrors of my swords.
I have arrived.

"Like a cripple, my retreat shall last only so long as I have not prepared a foot-ointment that travels across all the continents and is composed of the light from the jewel-stones in the crowns of every king.
Having thus resolved, he left his seat, dismissed the circle of courtiers, and abandoned the assembly hall, longing to begin his bath.
Rising, he performed the entirety of his daily routine as if he were in perfect health.
The day of the three worlds, its heat subsiding like the spreading pride of one who has fulfilled a vow, came to an end;
and then, as if terrified by the usurpation of its own authority, the sun, the lord of the day, departed for some unknown place, his splendor vanished;
and even the groves of lotuses began to contract as if out of fear, their humming bees hidden within.

Even the flocks of birds remained motionless, having withdrawn their fluttering wings as if out of fear and no longer appearing; while the entire multitude of people stood with bowed heads and joined palms, honoring the twilight that pervades the world as if it were a solemn vow;

and while the quarters of the sky became intensely formidable, enveloped by dense garlands of darkness as if encircled by a ring of iron ramparts provided by the guardians of the directions, trembling at the prospect of falling from their own stations—he did not remain for long in the assembly hall of evening.

As if being saluted even by the circles of lamps whose flickering flames were stirred by the breeze from the silken garments of the world’s kings bowing down, he dismissed his attendants and entered the bedchamber with the entrance barred to his followers.
There, lying on his back, he relaxed his limbs upon the surface of the couch;
and like a lover who has found his opportunity, the grief for his brother swiftly seized him, leaving him alone with the lamp.
With eyes closed, she beheld her elder brother as if he were still living within her heart;
her breaths rushed out one after another, as if searching for her brother’s life.
Covering her face with a flood of tears as if with the hem of a white silken garment, she wept silently for a very long time.
He reflected in his mind: "How indeed can such a transformation as this be fitting for one of such a form?
From my father, whose bodily frame was as hard as a mass of massive stones, the noble one was even more solid than iron ore, like a mountain."
And how could it be right for me, whose heart is destroyed by separation from my noble brother, even to breathe once more?
This is that very affection, devotion, or loyalty;
what fool, indeed, would imagine that my life could endure upon the death of my noble brother?
That such a unity vanished in an instant to some unknown place— by that very fate I have been separated from it without effort.
Though I wept for a long time with grief obscured by burning rage, I did not even weep aloud, being devoid of compassion.
In every way, the pleasures of living beings are as fragile as the threads of a spider's web and utterly hollow;
kinship is merely a bond for the journey through this world, such that even I, noble sir, now dwell as if a stranger while you remain at ease in heaven.
Alas, fate has brought about such a fruit—that this pair of brothers, whose hearts were blissful in their mutual bond of affection and who shared in happiness, have been torn asunder.

"And so, those very virtues of my noble brother—which once gladdened the world like moons—now burn me, as if they were the kindled funeral fires for one who has passed to another realm. With these and other such words, he lamented in his heart.
When the night had turned to dawn, he commanded the doorkeeper: "I wish to see Skandagupta, the superintendent of the entire elephant corps.
Then, being summoned by a succession of many men running forth simultaneously, [he arrived].
Leaving his own palace without his female elephant, he proceeded on foot in great haste; as the common folk were being cleared away by agitated staff-bearers,

he enquired at every step from the preeminent elephant-physicians— who bowed before him in every direction— regarding the condition of their choice elephants during the night, while the vast expanse of the quarters was filled with groves of bamboo thickets marked by the feathers of peacock tails, resembling the forests of the Vindhya range.
There were throngs of elephant-keepers who had arrived by chance, some engaged in crushing the bonds of elephants,

others running ahead with circles of men not under their control; some displaying handfuls of emerald-green grass, others entreating newly captured lordly elephants, and still others whose hearts were gladdened by having obtained the intoxicated tuskers they desired, approaching from afar to pay their respects and reporting the arrival of rut-fluid from their own elephants.
There were those petitioning for admission to the drum-beating ceremony;
those walking in front with long beards grown out of grief for the elephant lost through their own negligence;
and newly arrived mendicants running about in the hope of the joy of obtaining an elephant.
The scene was filled with groups of courtesans' attendants who had long awaited their opportunity and now raised their hands in greeting;
with rows of forest guards bustling with talk of serviceable female elephants, their banners of fresh sprouts fluttering in the wind;
and with throngs of mahouts holding aloft the wooden stakes for the tusks of newly captured wild elephants, while displaying the hides used in the training of those beasts.
There were also throngs of messengers from the elephant-forest guards, dispatched to report news of the movements of newly captured wild elephants;
they were reporting, while collecting fodder for the elephants, that at every village, town, and market, the heaps of elephant-rations had been inspected at every moment.
Creating a tumultuous clamor with his clusters of bracelets,
he— through the manifestation of great authority accumulated by his master’s favor and through his natural exercise of self-assurance— seemed to issue commands even while remaining indifferent,
as if ordering the oceans to provide an inexhaustible abundance of conch-shells from the ears of elephants.
As if plundering the mountains to seize the vermilion and red ochre used for his erotic body-paint;

as if wresting from the world-elephants the sovereignty over the quarters, like Airāvata himself; and as if destroying the earth’s pride in bearing heavy burdens with his footsteps—weighty as Mount Kailāsa when pressed by the weight of Śiva’s feet—he seemed, with the tossing of his two long, arm-like staffs that reached down to his knees and swayed with his gait, to be erecting a row of stone tethering-posts on both sides.

With his slightly protruding and hanging lower lip, which was as sweet as the taste of nectar and as tender as a fresh sprout, he seemed to entice Śrī Kāreṇukā with a morsel; he bore a nose-bridge as long as his own royal lineage;

and with the extreme tenderness, sweetness, whiteness, and breadth of his pair of eyes, he seemed to drink up the expanse of the quarters as if with a draught of the Milky Ocean, while his forehead was even more vast and wide than the slope of Mount Meru.
With his naturally fragile, curly locks— beautiful with their exceedingly long, dark, and soft luster as if they had grown thick under the constant shade of his unceasing parasol,
and playfully tossing like young creepers— he seemed to pluck away the lightless rays of the sun with his *barbaraka* head-ornament;
and though he had abandoned the work of the bow on the side of his enemies, the deep sound of his great virtues was heard throughout the ends of all directions.

Though he possessed every means of subduing even the most intoxicated elephants within himself, he remained untouched by pride; though possessed of great prosperity, he was full of affection; and though a king, he was composed of virtue.

Like elephants among those who give, he stood above the generous; like a noble woman, steadfast in devotion to a single husband and inaccessible to others, he had ascended to the status of a favorite of his lord, maintaining both a desirable mastership and an unassailable servitude.
He was the disinterested kinsman of the wise.
Skandagupta entered the royal palace, one who was a supporter of those who had no supporters and an un-purchased slave to the learned.
Even from afar, touching the ground with his head while grasping it with both lotus-like hands, he performed a salutation.
When he had sat down not too near, King Harṣa then said to him:
"The full details of this noble matter and of what we intend to do have already been heard by you."
"Therefore, let the elephant forces that have gone out for grazing be brought in quickly.
The fire of suffering from the humiliation of my noble lord does not tolerate even the slightest delay in our departure.
Thus addressed, he bowed and replied: "May my lord take note of what has been commanded; however, there is a small matter I wish to report out of devotion to my master."
May Your Majesty listen to this:

everything undertaken by Your Majesty is truly worthy of you— of a lineage born of the Puṣyabhūti dynasty, of innate nobility, of a pair of arms naturally endowed with splendor that extends like the trunk of a towering elephant, and of an extraordinary brotherly affection.
Even miserable worms known as *kākodarās* cannot endure an insult, much less those like you who are masses of splendor.
Your Majesty has already witnessed to some extent the wickedness of the evil through the account of Devarāja Vardhana;
indeed, such is the nature of the world, for in every village, every city, every region, every island, and every direction, the dress, appearance, food, speech, and conduct are all different.
Therefore, let this total trustfulness— born of a naturally straightforward heart and accustomed to the local customs of your own country— be abandoned.
Your Majesty hears daily many reports regarding the onset of the poison of negligence and vice.

Just as Nāgasena, born into a family of *nāgas*, was destroyed at Pajhāvatī after his secret mantra was overheard by a *sārikā* bird; and as Śrutatavarmā’s fortune crumbled at Śrāvastī after his secret was heard by a parrot;
and as Suvarṇacūḍa met his death at Mṛttikāvatī when his mantra was betrayed while he was dreaming.
And a beautiful attendant holding a golden fly-whisk, whose fingers were visible as reflections in the lines engraved upon the crest-jewel, met her death at the hands of the Yavana lord.
Furthermore, on a night thick with clouds, Vidūratha’s army, brandishing upraised swords, slaughtered Bṛhadratha, the King of Mathurā, who was greedily digging up a treasure hoard.
And the soldiers of Mahāsena, emerging from the body of an illusory elephant, brought about the downfall of the Lord of Vatsa, who was habituated to sporting in the elephant forests.
Mitradēva severed the head of Sumitra—the son of Agnimitra—who was excessively fond of dance—by means of his sword-blade, as if it were a lotus stalk, while he stood upon the stage like an actor.

The enemies of Śarabha, the lord of the Aśmakas, who was devoted to the lute, cut off his head with sharp swords inserted into the hollows of gourds and lutes used for musical accompaniment, while disguised as students of the Gandharva arts.
And they displayed their entire army under the pretext of a military review, while [Śarabha] himself was weak in wisdom.
The noble Puṣyamitra crushed his master, the Mauryan Bṛhadratha, who was devoid of an army;

and Kākavarṇa, out of curiosity for wonders, was carried away somewhere by a mechanical vehicle that traveled through the sky, constructed by a submissive Yavana, while the Śaiśunāga king was cut down by a sword at the edge of the city.

Vasudeva, the minister of Śuṅga— who was excessively devoted to the company of women and under the sway of the bodiless god of love— caused him to be deprived of life by means of Devībhūti’s maidservant’s daughter, who was disguised as the queen.

And the minister of the lord of Mekala had the king of Magadha, who was addicted to the cave of the Asuras, carried off through the subterranean tunnel of Mount Govardhana, which was delightful with the jingling sound of the jeweled anklets of countless beautiful women, back to his own territory.
And at the festival of Mahākāla, Tālajaṅgha, a *vetāla* driven mad by the wind of rumors regarding the sale of human flesh, slew Kumārasena, the youngest son of Pradyota and descendant of Puṇaka.

Furthermore, physicians in disguise, intent on the elixir of alchemy (*rasāyana*), produced consumption (*rājayakṣmā*) in Gaṇapati, the son of the King of Videha, after they had demonstrated the efficacy of their medicines to many men.
And Vīrasena, the king of Kaliṅga, became the death of his brother Bhadrasena by gaining the trust of women and remaining hidden within a secret wall in the queen’s chamber.

And while seated upon the mattress of his mother’s bed, the son became the cause of death for Dadhica, the lord of Karūṣa, who desired to consecrate another son as his successor. And the messenger of Śūdraka deprived Cakoranātha Candraketu, who was fond of clearing away [obstacles], of his life along with his ministers by removing him from his private quarters.

Furthermore, while Puṣkara was addicted to hunting and slaughtering wild buffaloes, the soldiers of the army of the lord of Campā, hidden in the thickets of tall reeds and marshy grass, took his life.
Furthermore, bards employed by his enemies, their mouths loud with cries of "Victory!", uprooted the foolish Maukhari Kṣatravarman, who was excessively devoted to women.
And in the enemy's city, Candragupta, disguised in the dress of a courtesan, destroyed the lord of the Śakas, who was lusting after another's wife.
Your Majesty has surely already heard of these instances where even negligence caused by women leads to the ruin of the heedless.
Just as Suprabhā, for the sake of her son’s kingdom, killed Mahāsena, the King of Kāśī, with parched grain (*lāja*) smeared with honey and *madhuraka* resin;
and as Ratnavatī, her pride of passion aroused by a pretext, killed Parantapa Jārūthya, the Lord of Ayodhyā, with a mirror whose edge was like a razor’s blade;
and as Devakī, infatuated with Devarāta, killed Devasena, the King of Sohnya, with an ear-lotus (*karṇendīvare*) whose nectar was touched by poisonous powder.
And with an ankle-ornament that showered the dust of battle, his beloved wife Ranti-deva was slain by Vairantya out of anger toward a co-wife;
and with a weapon concealed within her braid, Bindumati killed Vṛṣṇi, the son of Vinduratha;
and with a jeweled girdle smeared with poison, Hasavati slew Sauvīra, the son of Vīrasena.
"And with her face smeared with invisible ointment, she shall cause the daughter of Pūru, Soma, the lord of the Pūrus, to drink a mouthful of poisoned wine.
Having said this, she ceased speaking and departed to carry out her master's command.
The King, for his part, joyfully established all the arrangements for the kingdom.
Then, as King Harṣa—having thus made his vow—ordered the march for the conquest of the quarters, various omens appeared in the dwellings of his neighboring vassals whose lifespans had come to an end.
For indeed, there were swarms of black antelopes darting here and there like the restless glances of the messengers of Death standing nearby;
and the humming of swarms of honey-bees resounded, resembling the tinkling of the anklets of the Goddess of Fortune as she was departing.
For a long time, inauspicious jackals, emitting streams of fire from the cavities of their wide-gaping, distorted mouths, howled discordantly even during the day for the sake of ill omen;
meanwhile, forest pigeons with wing-edges tawny like the cheeks of young monkeys fell down as if their flight had grown heavy upon the flesh of corpses;
and the trees of the grove simultaneously bore out-of-season flowers, as if offering words of farewell.
The statues in the assembly hall wept violently, their breasts struck by blows from trembling palms;
the warriors saw their own headless trunks (*kabandha*) in the surfaces of their mirrors, as if their heads were whirling in terror at the imminent grasping of their hair;
and upon the crest-jewels of the queens appeared the footprints of their sovereigns, marked with the signs of the discus, the conch, and the lotus.
The maidservants' chowries suddenly slipped from their bud-like hands;
even during lovers' quarrels, the haughty women turned their backs and remained averted for a long time;
and the honey-drinking assemblies of bees were dispersed from the temples of the elephants.
As if fainting from the scent of the buffalo of Yama, even the horses did not graze upon the green fresh grass, though it was as abundant as a pillar;
nor did the pet peacocks dance in the palace, though they were coaxed by the music of cymbals played by girls whose hands were eloquent with moving bracelets.
Night after night, the pack of dogs howled loudly at the gateway without cause, their faces upturned as if their eyes were fixed upon the deer in the moon.
In the courtyards, Koṭavī passed the day with her forefinger trembling in a threatening gesture as she counted those whose lifespans had ended;
upon the mosaic floors, rows of young grass grew, rippling like the curved lines of a deer’s hooves;
and in the wine of their goblets, the faint reflections of the soldiers’ faces were seen, appearing with braided hair and the luster of kohl-less yet yellow-pigmented eyes.
The earth trembled as if terrified by the imminent theft of its very soul.

Showers of blood, possessing the crimson luster of blooming bandhūka flowers, appeared upon the bodies of the fallen heroes like splashes of red sandalwood juice used for the decoration of those condemned to death.

Blazing meteors fell in swarms, their limbs emitting dense, flickering sparks that scorched the clusters of stars, as if they were performing the ritual of circumambulation around the perishing Goddess of Fortune. They did not cease their descent.
"Even from the very beginning, a harsh whirlwind has been wandering about, snatching away chowries, parasols, and fans from every house like a female door-keeper," so it was said.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the King's Vow," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by Śrī Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
